In 430 BC, a virulent plague, the medical identity of which has been long debated, broke out in Athens, and spread rapidly through the population. Thucydides himself caught the plague, but survived to give a vivid account of the suffering. Very large numbers of Athenians died, and the imminence of death led to something close to a collapse of law and order. The disaster almost broke the Athenian spirit. There was a reaction against Pericles, who was tried and fined. An attempt was made to open peace negotiations with Sparta, but nothing came of it. In 429 Pericles died, himself a victim of the plague. The passing of the man who had been a major force in democratic politics for thirty years was bound to have a profound effect on Athens. Contemporary sources present Pericles' death as marking a sea change, after which things could never be the same, only worse. (World of Athens, 1.57)
